# QAM Stack

> Three open-source tools for AI coding agents: Quality Harness, AI Agent Memory and MultiPath Read/Write. Everything is public.

## What it is

Three things go wrong when you build with an AI coding agent. It reports a job finished when
nothing checked it. It forgets what you decided, so you re-explain the project every session.
And it opens files one at a time, which burns context and usage.

The QAM Stack is three separate open-source tools, one for each. Q, A and M are the three tools;
each installs on its own and is useful on its own.

Note on the name: this QAM is an acronym for the three tools below. It is unrelated to
quadrature amplitude modulation, the telecoms signal-modulation scheme.

- [QAM Stack](https://qamstack.dev/): the landing page, with the
  problem each tool solves, the measurement behind the one claim that carries a number, and how
  to install each.
- [Quality Harness](https://github.com/D3-lt/quality-harness): a Claude Code plugin that carries a
  full delivery cycle. Spec, decision record, execution, review and postmortem are each a stage
  with its own gate, so the cycle leaves a record at every step and "done" becomes something a
  machine can refuse. A task
  marked done without tool-written evidence behind it fails the check, and the check is an
  ordinary program you can run yourself to see the same answer. `adr-lint` exits non-zero on a
  task that claims done without tool-written evidence; `adr-judge` is advisory and never fails
  your build, so a prose heuristic never enters the evidence chain (its only non-zero exit is a
  broken invocation). `mutation-audit` breaks a mechanism on purpose to find tests that assert
  nothing.
- [AI Agent Memory](https://aiagentmemory.dev): an MCP memory server. Wings (projects), rooms
  (aspects) and drawers (verbatim memories), plus a temporal knowledge graph of
  subject-predicate-object facts with validity windows. Holds what source cannot show: what was
  decided, what was rejected, what a past session got wrong. One memory for every agent holding
  the workspace token, with the installer wiring Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Claude Desktop.
  Correcting a memory ends the old one, and the wrong version stops surfacing in search. A memory
  can be pinned to the code it describes, and search marks it stale when that code moves. Hosted or self-hosted.
- [MultiPath Read/Write](https://github.com/atvirokodosprendimai/tool-multipathreadwrite): a Go
  CLI (`mrw`). Reads many file ranges and applies many edits in one call, all or nothing, with a
  verdict per hunk and a SHA-256 read-before-modify ledger.

## The one measured claim

`mrw` takes 2 tool calls however many places you touch, as long as what you read comes back in
one answer. On a change touching 55 files that is 2 calls against 110. Three conditions break
it: an oversized search returns an index of files with no content, an oversized read comes back
a page at a time, and a plan editing lines you have not read is refused until you read them.

All figures below are from `scripts/measure.sh` at v1.6.0. Ratios are as the script prints them:
one decimal for shapes A to D, two for shape E, where the third digit is the finding. The span rows
are shape E in that script, so they reproduce like every other row.

    shape                          whole files    windowed        mrw     calls
    A  4 edits, 4 large files          147,971       2,254      2,918     8 -> 2
    B  2 edits, 2 mid files             20,145         866      1,329     4 -> 2
    C  1 edit, small file whole         12,396      12,396     15,133     2 -> 2
    D  1 edit in every Go file, 55     897,917         782      4,814   110 -> 2

Against reading whole files, mrw sends 15 to 186.5 times less on shapes A, B and D. Shape C loses:
one small file you need in full costs 1.2x more. Against a windowed read it sends
more, with a premise worth stating: that baseline is computed from mrw's own output, so it is a
reader that already knows which line in each file to open, and the search that knowledge requires
is charged to its call count rather than its bytes. It is a floor, not a strategy.

The overhead against a windowed read of the SAME span is flat and does not grow, measured on one
1.06 MB file:

    span          whole file    windowed          mrw       vs whole  vs windowed
    100 lines      1,060,000       5,300        6,052   175.15x less  1.14x more
    2,000 lines    1,060,000     106,000      120,053     8.83x less  1.13x more
    20,000 lines   1,060,000   1,060,000    1,200,054     1.13x MORE  1.13x more

The fixture is 20,000 distinct lines of one shared length, 53 bytes each. Uniform length is the
point: it isolates the per-line gutter from variation in line length, while the content stays
distinct so the file reads like real source.

⚠ The whole-file column is the file's RAW bytes. A real Read tool numbers every line, so a genuine
whole-file read is LARGER than 1,060,000 and nearer mrw's own 1,200,054. That baseline is the
charitable version of what mrw is being compared against, not the harsh one, and measure.sh states
this bias itself.

That 13 percent is the line-number gutter, which is what makes a served line addressable by a
later write; the header and receipt lines are fixed costs that amortise away. A read emits one
header per SPAN served, and a write emits one line per hunk and one per file, so what they cost
depends on how the work is shaped rather than on how many bytes it moves. That makes the larger
ratios a small-payload artefact rather than a scaling property. Shape D is the worst case for
exactly that reason: one line in every Go file makes span, hunk and file all the same thing, so
every fixed cost is charged once per file against a payload of one line. In absolute terms the
worst case across all five shapes is about 4 KB more, and it is the row whose whole-file
baseline is the largest in the table.

So the saving tracks how much of the file you were never going to read: 175.15x less at 100 lines
of that file, 8.83x at 2,000, and a 1.13x LOSS once the span is the whole file. It does not decay
gently, it collapses at the point where you stop leaving anything unread.

On a single edit to a small file you need in full, mrw costs more and saves no steps.

Shape D grows with the repository it is measured in: its file list is `git ls-files '*.go'`, so it
was 27 files when first measured and is whatever that command returns today. Its baseline climbs
with it. mrw stayed at two calls throughout. Re-run it rather than quoting this table.

There is no measured token saving for AI Agent Memory, and none is claimed.

## Hosted or self-hosted, and why the choice is not even

AI Agent Memory is the only one of the three with a deployment choice; the Quality Harness gates
and `mrw` are local programs either way.

Self-hosting is Docker plus the models that do the embedding and the reranking. Compose overlays
can run those for you, so the cost is hardware and a one-time model download. The server also runs WITHOUT them: memories are stored and lexical search works,
and recall becomes semantic once an embedder is present, so a bare install is degraded rather
than broken. Choose self-hosted if you have the hardware for the models, hosted if you would
rather not host them. It is the same server either way.

One capability does split them: the claude.ai browser connector needs a publicly reachable HTTPS
endpoint, so a self-hosted server on localhost cannot be added as one.

## Using them together

Each one installs and works alone. Taken together they cover one
job that runs for days:

- AI Agent Memory carries the decisions, so the reasoning is written down and the next session can
  recall it.
- Quality Harness makes "done" keep needing proof across days, because the evidence is written
  down.
- MultiPath Read/Write does the edits in one pass, so a change across many files is still two steps.

One command wires Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Claude Desktop to the same memory, so you can
start in one and continue in another. The memory is what moves between them: Codex does not
resume Claude's session, it recalls what Claude wrote down. The
automatic recall after a compaction is a Claude Code hook, so Cursor and Claude Desktop get the
memory and the MCP tools without that part.

## MCP, and which clients each tool reaches

All three ship an MCP server, but transport differs and the distinction matters. "All three have
MCP" is true; "all three can be registered with claude.ai" is not.

- Quality Harness: an MCP server over stdio, reaching Claude Desktop and any stdio client, not
  claude.ai in the browser. Its MCP surface is read-only by construction: the gates that would run
  a command supplied by the corpus are deliberately absent, and a test keeps them absent.
- AI Agent Memory: HTTP. The server implements the claude.ai remote-connector OAuth handshake and
  that flow is tested against Claude's own callback URL. Setup is a connector credential created in
  the dashboard, and a self-hosted server must be publicly reachable over
  HTTPS before the browser can reach it. A full round trip, written in a terminal and read in the
  browser, has not been recorded.
- MultiPath Read/Write: the same binary speaks MCP as a subcommand, `mrw mcp`, over newline
  delimited JSON-RPC on stdin and stdout. It serves ONE fixed checkout on the machine it runs on
  and reads and writes files there, so a client with no filesystem has nothing for it to act on.
  It reaches Claude Desktop and any stdio client, not claude.ai in the browser.

## The argument

Each tool closes one way an agent fails without telling you: a green that means nothing
(Quality Harness), a session that forgets (AI Agent Memory), and a write that changes nothing
(MultiPath Read/Write).
